answers.java_tx_design: We ran into transaction boundary issues a few times on our bidding platform's backend, which is in Java. Generally the approach was to keep transactions as short as possible and move slower external calls outside of them. I was involved in some of those discussions, though the team usually worked through the actual design together. It's something we revisited more than once as traffic patterns changed, and we generally found that keeping boundaries tight helped avoid the kind of locking problems that show up under load.
answers.java_ops: Operationally we dealt with the usual things — connection pool issues, some GC-related slowness here and there, that kind of thing. We generally addressed them by tuning configuration and keeping an eye on our monitoring dashboards. I was part of the team handling these, though it was often more of a group effort than any one person driving it. We made sure to follow up afterward to check things had actually improved.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't used Rust in production. answers.rust_boundary: I'd generally want to start with something lower-risk, somewhere that wouldn't have a big impact if something went wrong early on. answers.money_correctness: We generally handled duplicate requests using some kind of idempotency check before processing, and retries were set up with backoff so things didn't get hammered repeatedly. If something didn't match up, the usual approach was to look into what happened and correct it appropriately rather than just editing things directly. It wasn't really something I owned myself, more something the team handled together when it came up.
